title: The machine learning workflow I: time series

items.context:
You are building a table to forecast reactor pressure 30 minutes ahead
(h = 10). Each row is time t. Which feature makes the table leak?
items.why:
Everything in a row has to be known when the forecast is made. The channel's
past and the valves at t are known. The valves 30 minutes from now are not,
unless they come from a written plan, so using them is leakage stretched
across h rows.
items.true: Valve positions ten samples after t
false: Pressure nine samples before t
Valve positions at t
A rolling mean of pressure ending at t

items.context:
A table pools 500 simulation runs, one after another. The target is built
with `pl.col("xmeas_7").shift(-h)`, with no `.over(RUN)`.

What goes wrong?
items.why:
A negative shift reads forward. Without the run key it reads straight across
the boundary, so the final h rows of every run are asked to predict the
opening of a different, independent simulation.
items.true: The last rows of each run take their target from the next run
false: The first rows of each run lose their lag features
The target is h rows in the past instead of the future
Nothing, because the runs are sorted by sample number

items.context:
A channel's autocorrelation is zero at every lag above zero: it is white noise
around a setpoint. How does persistence compare with forecasting the mean?
items.why:
With rho_h = 0 the persistence error is sigma times sqrt(2), while the mean's
error is sigma. The last value adds its own noise to the next value's noise.
Separator level measures 1.415 on the fault-free runs.
items.true: Persistence is about 1.41 times worse than the mean
false: Persistence and the mean are equally good
Persistence is about 1.41 times better than the mean
Persistence wins at short horizons and loses at long ones

items.context:
For a stationary series, you read the autocorrelation at lag h off the ACF
before fitting anything. When will persistence beat the mean at horizon h?
items.why:
The mean's error is sigma and persistence's is sigma times sqrt(2(1 - rho_h)).
The two are equal at rho_h = 0.5. Above it, persistence wins. A positive but
small autocorrelation is not enough, and one step is not enough on white noise.
false: Whenever the lag-h autocorrelation is positive
Only when the lag-h autocorrelation is near 1
Whenever h is a single step

items.context:
A one-step forecaster for reactor pressure improves on persistence by 5 %.
A thirty-minute forecaster for the same channel improves on the better
baseline by 14 %. What explains the small one-step gain?
items.why:
At three minutes persistence is four times better than the mean, so there is
little left to win. The model earns most in the middle horizons, where
neither free guess is good. That small gap is also why an R-squared near 0.99
one step ahead says little about the model.
items.true: Three minutes out, persistence is already close to right
false: The one-step model was trained on fewer rows
One-step models cannot use lag features
The mean is the stronger baseline at one step

items.context:
At a 60-minute horizon on reactor pressure, persistence scores 8.87 kPa and
the mean scores 7.61 kPa. Which one should your model's skill score use as
its reference?
items.why:
Beating the worse baseline proves nothing. At an hour, pressure is weakly
related to pressure now, so the mean has overtaken persistence, and it is the
one the model has to beat.
items.true: The mean, because it is the better baseline at this horizon
false: Persistence, because it is always the standard baseline
Whichever makes the model's skill look largest
Neither, because skill scores need a fitted reference model

items.context:
Meese and Rogoff scored 1970s exchange-rate models out of sample. The models
fitted the historical data well. What did the comparison with a random walk
show?
items.why:
Their working paper says a random walk "would have outperformed all the other
models," including univariate models, a VAR, and combinations of forecasts.
A good in-sample fit said nothing about forecasting; only the baseline did.
items.true: The random walk forecast as well or better than all of them
false: The structural models beat the random walk at every horizon
The models won at one month and lost at twelve months
The comparison was impossible because exchange rates are not stationary

items.context:
A recursive AR(10) forecaster for reactor pressure matches the direct one at
three minutes, but at two hours it is worse than simply forecasting the mean.
Why does it fall apart further out?
items.why:
The recursive forecaster applies a one-step model h times, and each application
treats the previous guess as a measurement. Small errors become the next
step's input and grow. The direct forecaster trains on y[t+h] itself.
items.true: Each step feeds its prediction back in, so errors compound
false: The recursive model was trained on a different target
It uses fewer lags than the direct model
The mean is overfitted at long horizons

items.context:
Your one-step model uses pressure lags and the current valve positions. You
want to run it recursively ten steps ahead. What extra information does that
require?
items.why:
To feed y[t+1] back in, the model also needs u[t+1], which is not known at
time t. You must forecast the inputs or assume they stay put. A direct
forecaster uses only the inputs known at t and avoids the question.
items.true: The valve positions at each future step
false: The pressure at each future step
A separate model for every horizon
Nothing beyond what the one-step model already uses

items.context:
A teammate says: "On reactor pressure, direct beat recursive, so direct
forecasting is always the better strategy." What does the published evidence
say?
items.why:
Taieb and colleagues found that among single-model strategies the recursive one
almost always had the smaller error on the 111 NN5 series, and multi-output
strategies did best of all. The choice is measured on your own data.
items.true: Not always: on the NN5 series, recursive beat direct
false: Correct: direct wins on every published benchmark
Correct, but only for linear models
Not always: both strategies always give identical errors

items.context:
You forecast h samples ahead and split one series in time order, with the
test block starting right after the last training row and no gap. Which
training rows have targets that land inside the test block?
items.why:
A row at time t has target y[t+h]. For the last h training rows, t+h is past
the cutoff, so the model was trained on values it is then tested near. A gap
of at least h samples removes them.
false: Only the final training row
None, since the split is time-ordered
Every training row

items.context:
On single runs of reactor pressure, 30 minutes ahead, a random forest scores
4.32 kPa under shuffled KFold and 6.92 kPa under TimeSeriesSplit. Persistence
scores about 6.1. What should you report?
items.why:
Shuffled, each test row has neighbours from before and after it in training,
and a forest recalls them. The time-ordered score is the one you would see in
use, and it is worse than persistence.
items.true: The forest loses to persistence, so do not use it
false: The forest beats persistence by about 30 %
The average of the two scores, about 5.6 kPa
Neither, because the two splits disagree

items.context:
Pooled over 200 independent runs, a ridge model scores 4.74 kPa on a shuffled
row split and 4.71 kPa split by run. A classmate concludes the notes were wrong
about shuffling. What is the better reading?
items.why:
With that much data a linear model barely leans on a test row's few
neighbours, and K-fold is valid for a purely autoregressive model with
uncorrelated errors. The shuffled score is most dangerous on one short series
with a flexible model, where it flattered two models past persistence.
items.true: Never shuffling is a safe default, and this case sits at its boundary
false: Shuffling is always safe for linear models on any series
The by-run split must contain a bug
The runs must share neighbouring rows

items.context:
A residual detector alarms whenever a residual exceeds the 99th percentile of
normal residuals. The plant logs one sample every three minutes. Roughly how
many false alarms a day should you expect?
items.why:
The 99th percentile is exceeded by 1 % of normal samples by construction, and
a day holds 480 three-minute samples. Operators learn to ignore a detector that
cries wolf five times a day.
false: About 0.01
About 48
About 0.48

items.context:
After fault 1 begins, the one-step residual on reactor pressure leaves its
normal band, then returns inside it hours later, while the fault is still
present. Why?
items.why:
A residual reacts to surprise, not to distance from normal. Once the plant
settles into a new steady state, a one-step model predicts it well again, and
from the pressure channel alone nothing looks wrong.
items.true: The controller compensated, so the new state looks normal on this channel
false: The fault cleared itself partway through the run
The threshold was recalculated during the run
The model was retrained on the faulty data

items.context:
You want fewer false alarms from a residual detector, so you require three
consecutive exceedances before alarming. What do you give up?
items.why:
Lowering the false-alarm rate raises the detection delay. Three in a row
cannot fire until the third sample, so every alarm comes at least six minutes
later, and later still for a residual that flickers across the threshold.
false: The threshold no longer comes from normal data
The detector can no longer run without fault examples
Nothing, since false alarms and delay are unrelated
